title: What was your journey towards vibe-coding?
author: Disastrous-Screen296
selftext:
As the title says. Now as you know, ‘vib-coding’ is not an exact science or medium that that be taught or studied in a formal way, at least not in the traditional sense. So I’d like to know, what got you started in this field? did you feel it was risky given you will depend on a machine to build a structure you don’t fully comprehend? And how did you overcome the shortcomings of this medium. 

\[if your source of knowledge was YouTube, please do link the channel or playlist in the comments below.\]

replies.author: Wobstep
replies.body: Building a program by describing the features and logic through human language.

replies.author: Wobstep
replies.body:
Idk, maybe syntax. I imagine vibe coding to evolve and be seen the same people look at visual coding. Has pros and cons but visual scripting can do a lot for people who are used to it. 

Coding is typing in a programming language in text. You can have an ai assistant within the text editor and that's still coding but with a really good autofill. Vibe coding can be done in a text editor plugin or on a site like Google studio or Claude. I'm sure you know that difference but what I think really makes them distinct from each other is the building process. For the actual code, was the logic written with an agent but the design written through prompt in an agent chat session. That's what vibe coding is as far as I can tell. Really the line is starting to blur so who knows.

replies.author: HerbertGoon
replies.body: Hmmm is it like telling the ai something vague and vibing with the results?

replies.author: Wobstep
replies.body:
Kind of. I think the first idea is that the term itself "vibe coding" is too new to rigidly define. I will try anyway. 

I will assume you don't program or vibe code' but ignore whatever you know. 

There are many ways to write logic. Logic is the base of software but it needs to be in the form of something a computer/machine can understand. 

Normal programming: 
Pick a programming language. 
Learn the syntax. 
Figure out how to turn into machine code (compiling)
Write the logic. 
Test, debug, expand repeat. All using a language like C++, java or something. 

Notes:
These days, most people have their own personal workflow but most all coders use some form of auto complete. There are ai auto complete that will predict the next few lines of code. I do not consider this vibe coding because there is still a human touching programming language. 

Vibe coding:
Usually done in an ai focused environment, not a simple ide or text editor. Some are standalone editors running as an application (cursor, cline), some are cloud based and interfaced through a browser. (Claude, Google ai studio gpt etc). 
You could vibe code' using the normal chat gpt basic agent chat. Just ask for code or something and it will generate them and explain what to do if needed. 

You can go to Claude rn, go to their custom 'app builder'and type in plain English something like - "make me a simple webpage that has a button that will show a quote of a random author". It will generate the code and dependancies and create a packed folder with the whole webpage and then explain how to deploy it. 

I'm not really a web developer so this is what I do sometimes to make custom tools. Takes 20 minutes and I don't need to spend hours learning the stack. 

The last thing I will say is that the most difficult thing about what people call "vibe coding" and "coding" are relative. There are plenty of people who say it's fake and the results are too abstract for anything useful. First, as time goes on, this is just less and less true on the face, second, we have had new layers built on lower level programming since the beginning of programming. 

People forget that the typical programming languages they think are base real layer are an easily human readable abstraction to turn ideas of software into binary machine code. Vibe coding is just another layer of abstraction.

comments.author: Nice_Yesterday_4273
comments.body:
I'm still an amateur when working with Agents but to me two things seem to be true:

A: The better programmer you are to start with/the more knowledge you have about how and why you're trying to build using the stack you're using, the more efficiently/effectively you will be able to get what you want.

B: Managing an agent is a skill unto itself, comparable to any other skillset in programming. The reason you feel like it can't be taught is because (like programming) what works for you will depend on what you like, how your brain works, and what tools you are using to achieve your goals.

That doesn't really answer your question but it's what I think about when people bring up "vibe coding"

comments.author: w1zinvestmentss
comments.body:
Built a small game, and building a bigger game now. No coding experience, but I feel I'm generally great with technology and learning new programs. A tip I learned from YouTube that worked: when developing a game, first write an essay outlining everything about the game and outline your vision. Feed this to the ai so it knows your roadmap. I'm so impressed by AI's ability to remember my vision, and even prompt me along the way to add features I initially spoke about. I also found great features from asking ai, how can I make this better?
Vibe coding so far has been great, still have along way to go before it is production ready

replies.author: Defiant_Medicine_823
replies.body: I spitball with GPT for days on end about my game ideas, asking it for unrelenting criticism of every idea and concept until it stops tearing my shit apart. I then ask for it to split concerns into numbered sections, then generate full in-depth explanations of each section into a .md file one prompt at a time. I then ask it to put them all in a zip file to download then place it in my games file tree somewhere. From there I instruct the agent to follow that as a reference and after every prompt update a log file for that day on what we have implemented, changed and fixed.

replies.author: w1zinvestmentss
replies.body:
This is amazing. I am trying to finalize some of the core functionality, but this inspired me to have a dedicated brainstorming and critique session with my AI. I had a mini session and got a feature I would have never thought of. Since I work full time it's hard to schedule, but I will have a session like you described. Thanks for the feedback!
People insult ai, but it actually has amazing ideas and it's crazy patient. Can't image sitting down with a person for hours and getting such targeted feedback.

comments.author: thenomadcj
comments.body: For me it doesn't feel risky. I've always wanted to produce games and Ai is just like my worker in my studio who's job is to write code for me and debug. Also chucking in suggestions for features once and a while. And to bounce ideas off.

comments.author: thelionskywalker
comments.body: I watched a couple best practice videos and then started iterating on lovable at first. Now in codex.

comments.author: Defiant_Medicine_823
comments.body:
I started learning game dev like a month before the first dalle image generator was launched. Wasn't aware of gpt until a few months later, but my traditional learning how to code slowly shifted into:
"I wonder if AI knows how to solve this"


then,
"wow AI made this super easy"


Now:
"MAKE THING WORK STUPID BITCH I SAID TOP LEFT CORNER"

comments.author: OldTelephone320
comments.body: Started out just experimenting with small ideas instead of tutorials. It felt risky at first letting AI generate things I didn’t fully understand, but shipping tiny playable builds helped me learn faster than overthinking. Over time you start recognizing patterns and the black box feels less scary.

comments.author: National-County6310
comments.body: I do strict AI TDD. The ai explore and plan for about 2-3h if it a big one with me reviewing until I’m happy. Then implement in a stepwise manner using AI TDD. Always ensuring all test passes before moving forward. It’s a lot slower than vibecoding but I always know what is going on and can always extend. My experience when vibecoding is that I end up in a situation where AI fix one thing and 3 other breaks. For me TDD and strict Clean Architecture is key with heavy inspiration of microservices but built in one monolith. But with that said I do vibe code small skills and such on the side while developing main project. So end goal size is importat I would never vibe a 10k line code base! But a 800, sure no problem.

comments.author: Afzaalch00
comments.body: I got into vibe coding mostly out of curiosity. At first it felt risky relying on AI to generate systems I didn’t fully understand, but over time I realized it’s more about learning how to guide it than blindly trusting it. One thing that stood out to me was how compute heavy the whole process is. Generating assets, iterating mechanics, running models it all adds up. I’ve been running Tessala on my machine it uses idle GPU power for AI workloads and it made me appreciate how much infrastructure is quietly powering this shift. I don’t think vibe coding replaces understanding fundamentals, but it definitely changes how you approach building.
